title: From Maricarmen’s eviction to the general strike: how Spain’s youth are defying the housing crisis
content:
Almost two months after the eviction of Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose subsequent death sparked a movement, Spain’s housing encampments demanding change remain steadfast. Sofía Guerrero Orte, Alberto Pérez Madrona and Pablo Rodríguez Rodríguez, three university students involved in Seville’s encampment since the beginning, explain how the movement has grown and triggered an election, becoming the driving force behind Spain’s first general strike in 14 years.

“These young people today… they don’t protest like they used to…” They call us the “generación de cristal” or the “Glass Generation”.  They say we are fragile, but here we are protesting and resilient – because when glass breaks it cuts.

To many on the outside it may have looked like the Spanish housing protests happened overnight – an outpouring of grief and rage following Maricarmen’s eviction in September. But the lack of affordable housing has long suffocated students, young people, elderly people, single mums and marginalized populations, such as racialized groups – those of us who are already at higher risk of social exclusion.

title: Haiti: The governments of Haiti and El Salvador must ensure that the deployment of Salvadoran military personnel respects human rights
content:
Following clarification by Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the United Nations Secretary-General, that the vast majority of Salvadoran military personnel recently deployed to Haiti are not part of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), authorized by the UN Security Council, and therefore fall outside the mandate and monitoring mechanisms of the United Nations Support Office in Haiti (UNSOH), Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director, said:

“The Prime Minister of Haiti, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, and the President of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, must ensure that all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law. The Haitian Prime Minister’s commitment not to tolerate violations must translate into effective safeguards. Both governments must make public the agreement governing the deployment and explain how they oversee the deployed forces, what rules govern the use of force, to whom they are accountable, and how people can report possible violations without fear of reprisals.”

title: COP31: World leaders must break fossil fuels’ grip on climate policy and people’s futures.
content:
World leaders at COP31 in Türkiye must stop backing the fossil fuel industry and start delivering the rapid, equitable phase-out that science, human rights and international law demand, Amnesty International said today.

“The world is not running out of climate warnings. It is running out of excuses. After more than 30 years of climate negotiations, governments can no longer hide behind promises of future action or avoid confronting their fossil fuel industry allies. The climate crisis is not a failure of knowledge, but a failure of political courage. It is time to break the stranglehold of corporate power over political decision-making and end the fossil fuel era before it ends us,” said Marta Schaaf, Programme Director for Climate, ESJ and Corporate Accountability at Amnesty International.

The climate crisis is not a failure of knowledge, but a failure of political courage.

Marta Schaaf, Programme Director for Climate, ESJ and Corporate Accountability at Amnesty International

title: Paraguay: Institutional crisis demands a human rights-centred response
content:
In response to the financial and political crisis triggered by the initiation of resolution proceedings against a financial institution by the Central Bank of Paraguay (BCP), which has sparked public protests and led to impeachment proceedings against President Santiago Peña, Amnesty International calls on the Paraguayan authorities to ensure the protection of those affected, guarantee transparency and respect the right to peaceful protest.

“Behind this crisis are people who cannot access their savings, families facing uncertainty, and workers and pensioners whose rights may be at risk. The State’s response must put people at the centre, provide effective solutions and ensure that no economic or political interest takes precedence over their rights,” said Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Director for the Americas.

title: EU: Commission’s findings on TikTok “rabbit hole” effect must trigger fundamental changes to social media design
content:
Responding to the European Commission’s preliminary findings that TikTok is in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) because of the “rabbit hole” effect of its recommender system, Lisa Dittmer, Amnesty International Researcher on Children and Young People’s Digital Rights, said:    

“The Commission’s preliminary finding that TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed puts users’ wellbeing at risk is a welcome and urgently needed step in the fight for accountability and safer online platforms. Amnesty International’s research has repeatedly documented how TikTok draws some children into rabbit holes of depressive and suicidal ideation content. Young people and bereaved parents shared with us how TikTok’s feed normalized and exacerbated teenagers’ struggles with depression and self-harm. This should never have been allowed to happen.

title: Tanzania: Conviction and sentencing of opposition leader Tundu Lissu a travesty of justice
content:
Reacting to Friday’s conviction of Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu and his sentence of four years’ imprisonment for incitement, after he was acquitted of treason, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah, said:

“Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted. Today’s verdict and four-year prison sentence are the culmination of a deeply flawed process that was unjust from the moment of his arrest. He has already spent 577 days in arbitrary detention solely for the peaceful exercise of his human rights.

title: Israel/OPT: Israel must immediately release Palestinian farmer and land defender Ghassan Najjar
content:
In response to the Israeli military’s arrest of Palestinian farmer and land defender Ghassan Najjar during a pre-dawn raid on the village of Burin south of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank, on 27 October, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Research, Policy, Advocacy and Campaigns, said:

“Israeli authorities must immediately release Ghassan Najjar who was arrested solely because of his peaceful activism to protect the olive harvest season in Burin. Israeli intelligence agents had explicitly threatened Ghassan Najjar, co-founder of Burin’s Land and Farming Agricultural Cooperative, that he would be arrested if he did not stop his activism. His activism includes community organizing, supporting mutual aid among farmers through the cooperative, organizing an annual Kite Festival in the village and leading numerous cultural initiatives. Ghassan Najjar had been facing repeated threats since the start of the olive harvest season and their frequency intensified during the week prior to his arrest.

title: Hong Kong: Cruel Joshua Wong sentence a grim reminder of city’s disdain for human rights
content:
Responding to the 10-year sentence handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong for “colluding with foreign forces”, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks said:

“The Hong Kong authorities’ persecution of Joshua Wong continues with this latest national security conviction, which cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction.

“Joshua Wong’s bravery in speaking truth to power should be commended, but instead in Hong Kong it makes him a criminal. Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.

“The international community should not accept the continued criminalization of legitimate activism as the new normal in Hong Kong. Governments must continue to press for the protection of human rights and the release of those imprisoned solely for exercising their rights.

title: Belgium: ‘Divisive’ migration home raids law must be voted down by parliament
content:
Ahead of the vote in Belgian Federal Parliament on Thursday 5 November on whether to allow police raids on people’s homes for migration control purposes, including homes of people who may be hosting undocumented migrants, Dinushika Dissanayake the Deputy Regional Director of Amnesty International said:

“These proposals which allow for home raids are bound to sow fear and division. The bill before Belgium’s parliament gives police vast powers to enter people’s homes for migration control purposes, between the hours of 5am and 9pm and irrespective of whether children are present.

“This would not only cause a serious intrusion into people’s private and family life but also the bill fails to provide effective ways to appeal or challenge these decisions.

“Belgium has a strong tradition of showing solidarity towards migrant communities, with many people opening their doors and homes to offer beds, food and support – as is their prerogative. This will discourage people from doing so in future.

“These disproportionate powers are another cruel and coercive tool to create an increasingly hostile environment for migrants in Europe and for those showing solidarity with them.

title: South Sudan: Authorities, UN must investigate failure to protect victims of Abiemnom massacre
content:
• Government failed to protect residents of Abiemnom from attack
  • Both authorities and UNMISS had prior knowledge of an imminent attack
  • “The killing and destruction demand investigation,” Tigere Chagutah

    • South Sudanese authorities not only failed to protect residents of Abiemnom town from being massacred despite prior knowledge of a likely attack, but they have also failed to investigate and ensure accountability for those responsible, and justice and redress for victims and their families, Amnesty International said today in a new report.

    The organization also found that the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) knew that an attack was imminent but failed to take all preventive measures available to it, raising serious questions about the peacekeeping mission’s performance.

title: Thailand: Halt imminent forcible return of two Uyghur men to China
content:
Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said:

“Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Thailand must not repeat last year’s unlawful deportation of 40 Uyghurs, who were forced back to danger in China.

“These two men fled persecution only to spend more than a decade detained in Thailand. Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Returning them would expose them to the abuses they sought to escape.

“Both men have previously made clear to their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to being sent back. Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.

title: Peru: Closing the investigation into forced sterilisations perpetuates impunity
content:
Amnesty International condemns the decision by Peru’s Public Prosecutor’s Office to close the investigation into the forced sterilisation of 4,172 Peruvian women during the 1990s. This decision was taken pursuant to Law 32107, passed in 2024, which allows statutes of limitations to be applied to war crimes and crimes against humanity committed before 1 July 2002.

“Closing an investigation that the Public Prosecutor’s Office itself recognises as involving crimes against humanity is an affront to the victims, who have waited almost 30 years for justice. The Peruvian state cannot use a law that contravenes international law to block their path to truth, justice and reparation. This decision must be reversed and Law 32107 repealed to prevent it from continuing to be used as a tool of impunity,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International.

Closing an investigation that the Public Prosecutor’s Office itself recognises as involving crimes against humanity is an affront to the victims, who have waited almost 30 years for justice.”
